And so it was that in the time of the youth of the great destroyer Man, that a fleet of the heavens did come upon this the garden world: Eden. They fell upon this world with a maw that devours all it can see: in this state of pure gluttony they neglected Man as he walked upon their machines and learned their ways. His knowledge grew, quick and insatiable, soon he spoke with the vanguard of the heavens.

 

Their heed was not to be called as they ignored Man's reaching arms. They missed him operating their machines and creating his own buildings far from theirs. His creations became diverse and grew in creativity and forethought. Cities populated only by Man rose and fell as in rhythm with his whims. His eyes forever opened to greater things, drug him onward to create his own machines.

 

He built his own engines, powered by steam and fire, they roared in the valleys and took thirst from streams that he had rerouted. Mountains quaked as he bore into them and destroyed their foundations searching for elusive iron. Soon, his engines grew in complexity and sook no fire yet still the Vangaurd took no notice, ravaging the world of its resources and tearing it from the ground in great strips.

 

Man finally looked upon his world; his eyes sought out one thing he had seen. A thing that had been possessed by the Vangaurd and all the beasts that inhabited his land: a companion.

 

His thirst for a companion grew and he roamed his world in search of answers. He delved to the core of his world before returning with no change. He tore open the mountains and sought out their hearts of flame; when he returned, only one place remained...

 

He would talk to the gluttonous Vanguard, that lived on his world. His speech would open their eyes and ridicule would flow. Fury would take him and slaughter a few. Finally on a machine he knew, he would lie. His body strapped and tied, the surgical needles and saws would proceed. A night of screams, as bones were cut. He would emerge the next morning with a terrified look.

 

For hiding inside, a demon to him. Made from his very bones, a woman would emerge. She will walk and stumble before he catches her. Leading her away Man would finally feel happy. He would show her his world, now theirs. He would show her the machines that he built. He would show her the Vanguard. She will be confused. If this was their world, why could the Vangaurd abuse it?

 

The man will not know the answer, as the man had never asked the question. So the man will come to a realization, that which we all have already heard, man will rise up his vicious machines. Man will take them to the skies. The Vanguard will finally take notice, before they meet their demise.

 

But in his realizations, deep down inside, man will wish he never had taken a life. He wrecks his garden world Eden where he had once ran and played. He will take his wife away and begin a great journey. Here is where his story ends and a trillion others begin, for back on his garden world, in a tiny metal shell. Floating high above the world, a simple story is held.

 

Yes, the story is that of a being long ago locked away on this world. Entrapped to protect all species and to serve as a reminder. For he is the last of the great race called "man", they who ravaged the galaxy. His name is Adam, it said in the tiny shell, let him and his world lay fallow.

Here's another quick impression video for a game I won't be doing a full review for:

Stanley Parable
(Gameplay Video)

This game is a walking simulator built mostly around the narrator, who guides you through the "correct" path in the game, and narrates a story based on your obediance or lack thereof. It's decent if you enjoy exposition, and has some surprises - there are somewhere around 16 endings total - though after a couple hours I didn't care enough to find the rest of them. Most people probably won't discover all the content without a guide anyway - some of them are complicated or tedious to unlock.

 

So while it's well produced and humorous, I did eventually find myself wishing it had some legitimate gameplay - you can't even jump and most places are just a choice between two paths. So while it has a lot of decisions they all feel relatively shallow. The other thing I would have enjoyed is more visual endings. Only a couple had a specific cutscene at the end and this felt a lot more compelling and meaningful than the narrator giving you a speech and placing you at the beginning of the game. (Yeah, I get it, the whole game is a joke about game design - but still like the cutscene ending best)

 

Obviously I lean more toward visual experiences and puzzle solving than narrated stories, but it wasn't a bad experience. Just not something I loved quite as much as some other people seem to.
